entries.title: CPS despedirá a 760 maestros y tendrá 5 días de no asistencia para cerrar el déficit presupuestario
entries.summary: <p>Los líderes de las Escuelas Públicas de Chicago (CPS) anunciaron el miércoles planes drásticos para cerrar el enorme déficit del distrito escolar, que incluyen el despido de 760 maestros, 801 asistentes de maestros y 162 empleados de la oficina central y del área metropolitana.</p><p>El distrito también planea congelar el gasto a mitad de año y descansar al personal durante cinco días en los que no se suponía que los estudiantes asistieran, como los reservados para planificación, capacitación o la entrega de las calificaciones.</p><p>No pagar al personal durante cinco días le ahorraría al distrito alrededor de $85 millones. Para el maestro promedio, eso significaría una reducción salarial de $2,300, dijeron funcionarios del Sindicato de Maestros de Chicago (CTU), o alrededor del 2.3% de su salario.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f50000" name="module-f50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>CPS no ha despedido su personal temporalmente en una década, y el CTU y otros sindicatos de empleados probablemente impugnarán los recortes, ya que estos eliminarían algunos de sus aumentos salariales negociados.</p><p>Los funcionarios del distrito afirmaron que la congelación del gasto y los despidos temporales no se llevarán a cabo hasta la segunda mitad del año escolar y podrían evitarse si la Ciudad, el condado o el estado proporcionan más dinero a CPS, lo que probablemente sea un intento de captar la atención de los legisladores y otros funcionarios que hasta ahora han ignorado las súplicas por más financiamiento.</p><p>El miércoles, la superintendente de CPS, Macquline King, dijo que el distrito “enfrenta serios desafíos financieros” y que hay compensaciones en el presupuesto propuesto.</p><p>“Estos son impactos que son disruptivos para la educación de nuestros estudiantes, la experiencia de aprendizaje y, en última instancia, los resultados académicos que proyectamos para el próximo año”, dijo King, quien también es la directora ejecutiva del distrito.</p><p>Aún así, lo describió como un presupuesto “responsable” y “totalmente enfocado en los estudiantes” que evitaría que el distrito asumiera más deudas y pagos de intereses, lo que perjudicaría el gasto futuro en los salones de clase. Y destacó que algunos de los problemas financieros del distrito no son de su propia creación.</p><p>“Las inscripciones están disminuyendo, mientras que al mismo tiempo, las necesidades de nuestros estudiantes están en aumento”, señaló. “La financiación a nivel estatal y federal no ha mantenido el ritmo de estas necesidades que crecen”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Archivo Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>CPS debe aprobar un presupuesto equilibrado antes de finales de agosto, y los funcionarios han pasado meses intentando cerrar un déficit de $732 millones. Se espera que los miembros de la junta escolar voten sobre el presupuesto en su reunión del 30 de julio.</p><p>Wally Stock, tesorero de CPS y director financiero interino, dijo el mes pasado a los miembros de la junta que el distrito debería aprobar un presupuesto en julio porque está tan corto de efectivo que necesita urgentemente un préstamo a corto plazo para mantener el distrito en funcionamiento y pagar al personal. El distrito debe contar con un presupuesto aprobado para obtener esos préstamos.</p><p>Stacy Davis Gates, presidenta del CTU, dijo que el presupuesto “fracasó desde el principio” incluso antes de que CPS lo publicara oficialmente.</p><p>“Los estudiantes han tenido que aprender en clases abarrotadas, practicar con entrenadores que no reciben pago y ser asesorados por trabajadores sociales sobrecargados todo el año, y ahora ¿CPS piensa que puede planear una semana de despidos temporales y decirle al personal que los atiende que no tiene trabajo? Por favor”, destacó Gates en un comunicado.</p><h3>Los funcionarios de CPS esperan que la Ciudad o el estado intervengan para ayudar</h3><p>Los funcionarios de CPS están especialmente optimistas de que la Ciudad rescate al distrito escolar como lo hizo el año pasado sacando dinero de distritos impositivos especiales llamados TIF, como se les conoce al Financiamiento por Incremento de Impuestos. Cuando los funcionarios de la Ciudad deciden que los fondos TIF no son necesarios para proyectos de desarrollo económico, pueden declarar un superávit y distribuir ese dinero a entidades fiscales como CPS.</p><p>CPS confía en que la Ciudad le proporcione al distrito $200 millones en fondos TIF, más de lo que generalmente recibe CPS, pero menos de lo que obtuvo el año pasado. El distrito necesitaría 400 millones de dólares para evitar la congelación y los despidos temporales.</p><p>Sin embargo, los miembros del Concejo Municipala menudo tienen planes para cualquier dinero extra de los TIF y quieren retenerlo. Cuando el alcalde de Chicago, Brandon Johnson, declaró un superávit récord de $1,000 millones en TIF el año pasado, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/10/16/el-alcalde-brandon-johnson-propone-millones-para-las-escuelas-publicas-de-chicago" target="_blank" >los miembros del Concejo Municipal inicialmente se opusieron a dárselo</a> a CPS.</p><p>Y no está claro cuánto financiamiento TIF podría estar disponible para CPS. La Ciudad no anuncia cuánto planea declarar como superávit hasta el otoño.</p><p>Un grupo creciente, que incluye al CTU, otros sindicatos, miembros de la junta escolar y funcionarios de CPS, está presionando al gobernador JB Pritzker y a los legisladores estatales para que convoquen una sesión especial destinada a aumentar la financiación educativa. Dicen que no es una solicitud infundada, ya que los legisladores estaban dispuestos a aprobarla para negociar el estadio de fútbol de los Chicago Bears.</p><p>Hasta ahora, los líderes estatales han rechazado esos llamados. Pero King dijo que aún tiene esperanzas de que el estado y la Ciudad respondan.</p><p>“Esto requerirá un llamado unificado a la acción”, señaló. “Mi esperanza es que en los próximos meses, todos nos unamos en un trabajo conjunto de defensa... en servicio de los niños de Chicago”.</p><h3>Dos años de presupuestos ajustados para CPS</h3><p>El anuncio de que CPS despide a 760 maestros no sorprendió. Cuando en mayo los directores recibieron sus asignaciones de personal para el año escolar 2026-27, se les informó que el distrito aumentaría la proporción de estudiantes por maestro para ahorrar dinero. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/05/12/cps-plans-cut-teacher-positions-raise-class-sizes-shrink-723-million-deficit" target="_blank" >Un análisis de WBEZ reveló</a> que probablemente se traduciría en alrededor de 700 maestros menos.</p><p>El distrito escolar también está despidiendo a algunos maestros y asistentes debido a la disminución de las inscripciones o a una reducción en cuántos apoyos y servicios de educación especial necesitan los estudiantes en las escuelas individuales.</p><p>Muchos de los maestros y asistentes que están perdiendo sus trabajos ya fueron informados por sus directores, y las notificaciones oficiales de despido salieron el miércoles. Los funcionarios del distrito señalan que la mayoría del personal despedido temporalmente es recontratado por CPS, porque surgen puestos vacantes cuando el personal renuncia o se retira.</p><p>Ben Felton, jefe de talento, dijo que el número total de asistentes y maestros está en realidad aumentando, en gran parte debido a las necesidades en aumento de educación especial en todo el distrito.</p><p>El CTU envió a los líderes de CPS una carta el miércoles en la que solicitaba negociar sobre los despidos planeados. La carta pidió al distrito que tomara acciones legales contra el tesorero del Condado de Cook, ya que la oficina se ha retrasado en la liberación de los impuestos sobre la propiedad de los que CPS y otras entidades gubernamentales dependen para pagar a su personal.</p><p>CPS también enfrentó un enorme déficit en el presupuesto del año pasado. Los funcionarios cerraron ese vacío de $734 millones después de meses de debate contencioso mediante recortes de personal, refinanciación de deudas y aprovechando fuentes de financiamiento únicas, como $550 millones en fondos TIF de la Ciudad.</p><p>CPS despidió a 500 conserjes, 250 trabajadores del comedor, más de 100 guardias de cruce y decenas de empleados de oficina. El distrito también recortó al personal de la oficina central e instituyó una congelación de contrataciones.</p><p>En ese momento, el director de presupuesto de CPS dijo que ya no había más “soluciones fáciles” para recortar y que los futuros recortes tendrían que impactar en los salones de clase.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: New cholesterol-busting pill, costly but powerful, gets FDA's OK
entries.summary: <p>The federal Food and Drug Administration has approved a first-of-its-kind pill that sharply reduces artery-clogging cholesterol in people who remain at high risk of heart attacks despite taking statins.</p><p>The pill, named enlicitide, will be sold under the name Lipfenrda. Taken daily, it helps rid the body of cholesterol in a way that until now could be done only with injected medicines and significantly more than statins do.</p><p>Expected to be available within weeks, it won't come cheap. According to Merck, the manufacturer, its list price will be $10.50 a day, which. Depending on whether and how much insurers decide to cover it, that could limit the number of people it might reach.</p><p>Still, it will offer an easier-to-use option for millions of people.</p><p>Statins block some of the liver’s production of cholesterol and are the cornerstone of treatment. Even taking the highest doses, though, many people need additional help to lower their LDL, or “bad,” cholesterol enough to meet medical guidelines.</p><p>In a major study, more than 2,900 high-risk patients were randomly assigned to add a daily enlicitide pill or a dummy drug to their standard treatment. The enlicitide users saw their LDL cholesterol drop by as much as 60% over six months, researchers reported earlier this year in the New England Journal of Medicine.</p><p>There are other pills that can be taken in addition to the usual treatment, statins, to fight cholesterol. "But none come close to the degree of LDL cholesterol-lowering that we see with enlicitide,” according to Dr. Ann Marie Navar, a cardiologist at UT Southwestern Medical Center who led the study reported in February.</p><p>One caveat: The pill must be taken on an empty stomach.</p><p>Heart disease is the nation’s leading cause of death, and high LDL cholesterol, which causes plaque to build up in arteries, is a top risk factor for heart attacks and strokes. While an LDL level of 100 is considered fine for healthy people, doctors recommend lowering it at least to 70 once people develop high cholesterol or heart disease — and even lower for those at very high risk.</p><p>Statin pills like Lipitor and Crestor, or their cheap generic equivalents, are highly effective at lowering LDL.</p><p>For additional help, some powerful injected drugs work differently, blocking a liver protein named PCSK9 that limits the body’s ability to clear cholesterol from blood. But they are even more expensive than Lipfendra. And only a small fraction of people who could benefit from PCSK9 inhibitors use them. While prices for the costly shots have dropped, some people are averse to administering shots.<br></p>

entries.title: How Bulls might replace late TV analyst Stacey King — here are 5 candidates
entries.summary: <p>There’s no replacing Stacey King, but the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> will have to try.</p><p>King, the team’s longtime TV analyst, shockingly died June 7 at 59. After their Summer League season ends Friday, the Bulls’ next games will come in October in the preseason. Chicago Sports Network figures to carry them, so the Bulls will need an analyst in place.</p><p>No one will be able to duplicate King’s enthusiasm and catchphrases, and that’s OK. No one would expect that. But because of the enormous shoes the next analyst will fill, the Bulls are leaning toward using several analysts this season to ease the pressure on them, the Sun-Times has learned.</p><p>That would be prudent. The Bulls didn’t think they needed to keep a list of potential successors to King, and because he rarely missed a game, he didn’t have backups like play-by-play partner Adam Amin does.</p><p>But there are plenty of options. Requirements aren’t set in stone, but pluses include having played for the Bulls, having won a championship and having Chicago ties. Bulls president and CEO Michael Reinsdorf and executive vice president for brand and public affairs Susan Goodenow will make the final decision.</p><p>If the Bulls go the rotation route in hopes that a fan favorite emerges, they’ll need to avoid making the mistake the Blackhawks made when they auditioned successors to Hall of Famer Pat Foley several years ago. All the different voices annoyed fans and took away from the broadcasts. A rotation of three or four analysts over 82 games could work for the Bulls.</p><p>That said, they’ll be forced to use two replacements when Amin misses time in the first half of the season to call NFL games for Fox. An analyst with national commitments could pose scheduling problems for the Bulls, requiring them to have backups for both play-by-play and analyst roles. Amin, whose profile is growing nationally, has two years left on his Bulls contract.</p><p>Here’s a list of candidates to be a Bulls TV analyst, including my personal pick (hey, it’s my job):</p><h3>Kendall Gill</h3><p>The longtime Bulls studio analyst has never been a game analyst. If he wants to give it a shot, now’s the time. Gill has always provided outstanding analysis in the studio, and he tells it like it is. The Chicago native, former “Flyin’ Illini” star and 15-year NBA veteran played one season for the Bulls, in 2003-04. Otherwise, expect Gill to be back in the studio with host Cam Smith.</p><h3>Robbie Hummel</h3><p>The Bulls are interested, and Hummel is interested — but it probably won’t work. Hummel, one of the best analysts around, has too many national commitments calling college basketball to make himself available to the Bulls permanently. A package of games as part of a rotation might work, but for the full-time job, Hummel would have to take a pay cut to come here. The Valparaiso, Indiana, native filled in on Bulls TV and radio in 2022.</p><h3>Sarah Kustok</h3><p>The Chicago-area native and former DePaul player began her broadcasting career at Comcast SportsNet Chicago. She became the first female full-time analyst for an NBA team’s local TV broadcasts in 2017, when the YES Network promoted her for Nets games. Kustok also calls the WNBA for NBC and USA. She’s a star in the business. Would she want to come home? The Bulls would love to have her.</p><h3>Will Perdue</h3><p>He’s my pick, and he checks all the boxes. He was on the Bulls’ first three-peat teams, he was fantastic on the studio shows with Gill and former host Jason Goff and he was a game analyst before, having worked with the late, great Jim Durham. The Bulls might bristle at his criticism, but that’s what fans want. Broadcasters can’t pull the wool over fans’ eyes in Chicago; they’ll get called out. Of everyone on this list, Perdue would fit in seamlessly.</p><h3>Scott Williams</h3><p>Another member of the Bulls’ first three-peat teams, Williams has been the analyst for Grand Canyon University in Phoenix and part of ESPN’s college basketball coverage out west. Previously, he was a TV analyst for the Cavaliers, Bucks and Suns. Williams has a personality similar to King's that could endear him to fans quickly. He’s also a motivational speaker, which could come in handy during another rough season.</p><h3>Remote patrol</h3><p>Two of the White Sox’ three games this weekend against the Blue Jays will appear on streaming services.</p><p>The game at 6:15 p.m. Friday will air on Apple TV, with <b>Alex Faust</b>, analyst <b>Eric Hosmer</b> and reporter <b>Tricia Whitaker</b> on the call. The game at 11:15 a.m. Sunday will air on Peacock, with <b>Dave Flemming</b>, analysts <b>Dan Plesac</b> and <b>Caleb Joseph</b> (a former Jays catcher) and reporter <b>John Fanta</b> on the call. That game will simulcast on NBC Sports Network.</p><p>• The Cubs’ Marquee Sports Network will air the dedication of the Champions Gate outside Wrigley Field live at 10 a.m. Saturday. It will be replayed at 11.</p><p>• <b>Jon Sciambi</b>, analysts <b>Eduardo Perez</b> and <b>Adam Ottavi</b>no and reporter <b>Buster Olney</b> will call the Tigers-Cubs game at 7:10 p.m. Wednesday on ESPN. “Baseball Tonight” will precede it at 6.</p><p>• <b>Jack McMullen</b>, the Marlins’ radio voice and The Score host <b>Matt Spiegel’s</b> nephew, was named the lead voice for the CW’s coverage of entries.title: Sold! 7-ton glass desk designed by Frank Gehry fetches $243,000 at auction
entries.summary: <p>The 7-ton glass desk designed by the late architect Frank Gehry for the lobby of the Inland Steel Building sold at auction Wednesday for $243,200.</p><p>The 16-piece ensemble, made of emerald-colored glass and named Icehenge, had been anticipated to fetch <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/07/07/loop-glass-desk-designed-frank-gehry-7-tons-auction-inland-steel-building" >between $100,000 and $200,000</a>. </p><p>Freeman's, which handled the online auction of the desk, listed the winning bid on its <a class="Link" href="https://freemansauction.com/auction/6517-art-design/lot/108" target="_blank" >website</a>.</p><p>While Freeman's made known the successful bid for the one-of-kind item, the auction house was mum on the identity of the lucky paddle-raiser. The company didn't respond to requests for comment.</p><p>The auction result means the likely end to a small but noteworthy chapter in Chicago's storied history of architecture and design.</p><p>Gehry — whose portfolio includes internationally renowned structures such as the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, Spain, the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles, and Millennium Park's Pritzker Pavilion and BP Pedestrian Bridge — held a nearly lifelong admiration for Chicago's sleek Inland Steel Building at 30 W. Monroe St.</p><p>From 2005 to 2007, the architect had a small ownership piece of the Inland Steel Building, a 19-story skyscraper designed by SOM and built in 1958.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c40000" name="image-c40000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fbb72e1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7384x4144+0+390/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2F7e%2F18377e5d46638574b17545e13ce8%2Fgehry-260707-07.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/813d510/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7384x4144+0+390/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2F7e%2F18377e5d46638574b17545e13ce8%2Fgehry-260707-07.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b73206a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7384x4144+0+390/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2F7e%2F18377e5d46638574b17545e13ce8%2Fgehry-260707-07.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Exterior of the Inland Steel Building at 30 W. Monroe St.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Working with John Lewis Glass Studio, now <a class="Link" href="https://www.christisonlewis.com/about" target="_blank" >Christison Lewis</a>, in Oakland, California, Gehry created the 15,000-pound desk unit specifically for the Inland Steel lobby.</p><p>The work — a staffed and functioning security desk — was installed in the building in 2012.</p><p>Gehry <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2025/12/06/architect-frank-gehry-obituary-millennium-park-music-pavilion-foot-bridge-dies-96" >died in 2025</a> at age 96.</p><p>Icehenge is as much sculpture as it is furniture, with the same billowing, sail-like quality found in many of Gehry's designs. But the work is also visually untamed, jagged and unpredictable.</p><p>"It does look like an explosion in a glass factory, kind of," the Los Angeles architect told Chicago architecture critic Blair Kamin in 2013. "If you actually had an explosion at a glass factory, apart from everyone getting killed, it would be pretty exciting visually."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Robert Lewandowski’s Fire debut delayed after poor air quality forces postponement vs. Vancouver
entries.summary: <p>Robert Lewandowski’s MLS coming out party will have to come on another day.</p><p>The Fire announced that Thursday’s match against the Vancouver Whitecaps at Soldier Field was postponed because of the poor air quality alert in Chicago. Polish superstar Lewandowski was expected to make his MLS debut in the match. </p><p>The match will be played on Tuesday, Oct. 6. A post-match concert by the DJ duo Two Friends will also be rescheduled. </p><p>Smoke from a Canadian wildfire made it dangerous for anyone to be outside for long periods of time, government officials warned.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/16/wildfire-smoke-prompts-air-quality-alert-for-most-of-chicago-area-to" >‘Hazardous’ Canadian wildfire smoke prompts air quality alert for Chicago. Here’s what you should know.</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>"We share our fans' disappointment, especially given the excitement surrounding our first match back following the FIFA World Cup break and the anticipation of welcoming more than 40,000 fans to Soldier Field," Dave Baldwin, the Fire's president of business operations, said in a statement. "With a marquee matchup against Vancouver, the anticipated home debut of Robert Lewandowski, and the Two Friends post-match concert, tonight was expected to be a special evening at Soldier Field. While we know this decision is disappointing, health and safety must come first."</p><p>The city closed its beaches and all 50 outdoor swimming pools because of poor air quality. The Chicago Park District canceled all outdoor activities that couldn’t be moved inside.</p><p>The captain of the Polish national team, Lewandowski, 37, last played for Spanish powerhouse Barcelona. After starting his professional career in Poland, Lewandowski also suited up for German titans Bayern Munich and Borussia Dortmund, winning the 2020 Champions League with Bayern.</p><p>Lewandowski is the latest big-name signing for MLS, joining Lionel Messi in Miami, Thomas Muller in Vancouver and Son Heung-Min with LAFC.<br></p>

entries.title: At Lincoln Park Zoo, lots of people, but not many animals. Why? The heat, of course.
entries.summary: <p>The lion enclosure was empty. The gorillas, gone. The rhino, which can typically found standing stolidly in the old elephant enclosure, looking like a beast from mythology, was standing somewhere else, out of view.</p><p>My wife and I were strolling the Lincoln Park Zoo late Saturday afternoon, a beautiful day, the zoo crowded. With people that is. With animals, not so much.</p><p>"Is it me," I wondered aloud, "or is something missing?"</p><p>We'd seen a scattering of pink flamingos. And that's about it. </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8e0000" name="module-8e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>Suddenly, the animal art the zoo has on display everywhere took on a malign significance — here are the sort of beasts you might see. If they were here. There were plenty of privacy hedges, barriers to keep the crowds back. I knew that while you might want to see animals, animals don't necessarily want to see <i>you</i>.</p><p>"Maybe because it's late in the day," my wife speculated. The animals were tired from a long day of flaunting themselves to their endless stream of guests, capering and cavorting. They were resting now, renewing themselves for tomorrow's efforts. I thought of that Charles Addams cartoon showing a disappointed man and boy at the front door of a zoo, while a bear, ostrich, moose and gorilla exit a side door, the gorilla putting on his hat.</p><p>"Sorry folks," the zookeeper says, "we quit at five."</p><p>One way to find out. I queried the zoo.</p><p>"A somewhat unique feature about Lincoln Park Zoo is the commitment we’ve made to giving all animals in our care the choice and control over where they want to be at any point in the day," wrote Anna Cieslik, PR and communications manager. "This means that if the weather isn’t great, or if they’re just not feeling like being around people for the time being, they can always retreat to their indoor habitats. As Chicago dives headfirst into the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/14/near-record-breaking-heat-expected-as-sizzling-heat-wave-continues" >hottest days</a> of the year, as was the case Saturday during the daytime, animals might be choosing to spend more time indoors. While that’s a bummer for someone hoping to see a lion or brown bear, it means they’re receiving the best welfare possible."</p><p>Well, that's a comfort. And my long experience with the zoo might have sharpened my disappointment. I remember going there with the boys — walking, from Pine Grove Avenue, pushing the massive double stroller we called "The Bus." The roar of Adelor the lion, echoing across the zoo. The elephants, gone since 2010, massive and very much there.</p><p>On Saturday, we plunged into the reliable Regenstein African Journey, where a giraffe did give us the briefest glance before bolting for cover. So maybe it's me — maybe I repel animals somehow. Though I did have a bonding moment with a quartet of guinea hens. My wife noted that as I studied them, they seemed to be edging closer. We also saw a pygmy hippo, sprawled and resting, looking like the largest slug ever.</p><p>"Regenstein African Journey is home to some of my favorite animals at the zoo — the meerkats," said Cieslik. "There are two mobs of meerkats here that are pretty reliably on view watching over their habitat. You’re sure to spot some avian delights at McCormick Bird House, where the free flight exhibit will get you up close and personal with some of our feathered residents. Regenstein Center for African Apes is also a fun building to check out in the afternoons, as the family gorilla troop is often preparing for bedtime by then. Great apes are big nest makers, and you can spot them building their elaborate beds for the evening starting in the afternoon."</p><p>Didn't notice any meerkats, though there were plenty of Madagascar hissing cockroaches. And later, we did see some lovely snow leopards.</p><p>Is time of day a factor?</p><p>"Mornings at the zoo are usually the best time to swing by if you want to see animals out and active," Cieslik said. "That’s when animals like the lions and African painted dogs might receive meaty bones or a hide-on carcass feeding, plus it’s cooler in the mornings. This is also a great time to see crepuscular animals like the red pandas, who are most active at dawn and dusk. If you manage to make it out to an after-hours event at the zoo in the evening, that’s also a great opportunity to see crepuscular animals and even some nocturnal ones like the aardvark!"</p><p>"Crepuscular" — good word. "Related to twilight." </p><p>Wondering if I'm alone here, I asked my Facebook hive intelligence if anyone had been to the zoo and felt similar.</p><p>"Sometimes it's just like walking around a park with exhibits of the kinds of habitats animals would live in if they were here," said Peter Nee, summarizing the views of several dozen others.</p>
entries.author: Neil Steinberg

entries.title: Defensores de inmigrantes en Chicago exigen abolir ICE tras tiroteos mortales en Houston y Maine
entries.summary: <p>Tras los tiroteos mortales que involucraron a agentes del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) en Houston y Maine, los defensores de los derechos de los inmigrantes en Chicago afirman que los incidentes subrayan sus demandas de abolir ICE y de restringir las tácticas de aplicación de la ley que ya han causado daño en Illinois.</p><p>Los dos tiroteos ocurrieron con menos de una semana de diferencia, ambos durante intentos de detenciones de tráfico, intensificando el escrutinio sobre las tácticas utilizadas en la aplicación de la ley de inmigración. La administración de Trump reaccionó con señales contradictorias sobre el uso de las detenciones por tráfico de ICE, con funcionarios de la administración <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/07/15/ordenan-a-ice-suspender-la-mayoria-de-paradas-de-vehiculos-tras-2-tiroteos-mortales" target="_blank" >que dirigieron a los agentes a suspender la mayoría de las paradas de vehículos</a> antes de que el presidente Donald Trump dijera que quería que continuaran.</p><p>Los incidentes han resonado entre los defensores del área de Chicago, que señalan el asesinato en septiembre de Silverio Villegas González, quien fue fatalmente baleado por un agente de ICE durante un intento de detención de tráfico en Franklin Park, y el tiroteo en octubre de Marimar Martínez a manos de un agente de la Patrulla Fronteriza.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-920000" name="module-920000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Para los defensores de los derechos de los inmigrantes, el debate sobre las detenciones por tráfico es solo una parte de lo que describen como un enfoque más amplio de la aplicación de la ley de inmigración.</p><p>Brandon Lee, portavoz de la Coalición por los Derechos de los Inmigrantes y Refugiados de Illinois (ICIRR), dijo que limitar una táctica no aborda lo que los defensores consideran el problema raíz: los esfuerzos de la administración de Trump por infundir miedo en las comunidades inmigrantes y llevar a cabo deportaciones masivas.</p><p>"Todas las tácticas que Trump está utilizando, ya sean detenciones de tráfico, detener a personas mientras van y vienen de la corte o detener a personas en registros, todas tienen el mismo resultado final: la separación de familias y la interrupción de las comunidades. Y, en algunos casos, es fatal", dijo Lee.</p><p>"No lo vemos como si el abandonar una táctica haría que nuestras comunidades fueran más seguras, porque todavía tienen miles de millones de dólares y una amplia gama de otras tácticas a su disposición".</p><p>Si bien Lee dijo que los defensores continúan pidiendo la abolición de ICE, eso sigue siendo poco probable bajo la administración de Trump.</p><p>Mientras tanto, dijo, el Congreso y los funcionarios estatales pueden establecer "límites claros sobre ICE. Eso podría incluir medidas de protección para inmigrantes cuya autorización de trabajo o de las protecciones contra la deportación estén en riesgo.</p><p>Lee señaló que los defensores también quieren un procesamiento oportuno de las renovaciones de DACA y de las protecciones para inmigrantes que podrían perder su estatus legal debido a cambios en la política federal, incluidos los haitianos y otros cuyos estatus de protección temporal (TPS) pueden ser revocados.</p><p>A nivel estatal, Lee destacó que es importante que los funcionarios hagan cumplir dos leyes de Illinois: una prohíbe a las fuerzas del orden locales cooperar con las autoridades federales de inmigración, y la otra impide que los agentes federales de inmigración realicen arrestos civiles en las cortes.</p><p>Kayla Nguyen, copresidente de medios de la Alianza de Chicago Contra la Represión Racista y Política (CAARPR), dijo que los tiroteos recientes reflejan lo que su grupo considera un patrón más amplio de prácticas de la aplicación de la ley de inmigración que perjudican desproporcionadamente a las comunidades negras y latinas.</p><p>Su grupo, que organizó una vigilia el miércoles por la noche para las víctimas en Houston y Maine, ha exigido el fin de lo que llaman detenciones de tráfico por motivos falsos, lo que significa, según su grupo, que los agentes detienen a conductores por una infracción menor como excusa para buscar crímenes más graves.</p><p>"Creemos que las detenciones de tráfico [por parte de ICE] deben terminar, punto", dijo Nguyen. "Por supuesto, estos tipos de asesinatos no están sólo relacionados con las detenciones por tráfico. Están vinculados a una represión más amplia que existe contra los derechos de los inmigrantes en general".</p><p>Ella coincidió con Lee en que los funcionarios estatales necesitan seguir haciendo cumplir las leyes estatales que protegen a los inmigrantes y mitigan el uso de la fuerza por parte de ICE.</p><p>El Grupo Legislativo Latino de Illinois, compuesto por 18 miembros, también condenó los tiroteos recientes y pidió poner fin a lo que describió como una escalada en la aplicación de la ley de inmigración en Illinois. El grupo expresó su preocupación por la actividad de ICE cerca de las cortes.</p><p>"La persecución de nuestra comunidad inmigrante debe parar", dijo el grupo en un comunicado. "ICE necesita irse de nuestras ciudades y dejar en paz a nuestras comunidades. Debemos levantarnos y luchar contra los extremistas en nuestro país, porque nuestros vecinos inmigrantes merecen sentirse protegidos y seguros en nuestras comunidades".</p><p>El senador estadounidense Dick Durbin, demócrata por Illinois, también pidió responsabilidad tras los tiroteos en Houston y Maine, diciendo que debería haber "investigaciones completas, justas e independientes" sobre las muertes. Instó al Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) a no deportar a los testigos antes de que puedan participar en las investigaciones.</p><p>"Debemos contener los abusos de ICE antes de que se pierda otra vida", agregó.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Indiana family sues Amazon after 2025 crash that seriously injured 16-year-old boy
entries.summary: <p>All 17-year-old Lucas Bradshaw wants is to get back on the baseball field.</p><p>But a crash last year left the high school student with severe brain injuries, putting his dreams on hold and beginning a long road to recovery.</p><p>Lucas Bradshaw, who was 16 at the time, was traveling with his team to a baseball game on May 8, 2025, when their bus was struck by a box truck driven by Shawn Akison, 42, who was traveling at 73 mph and under the influence of fentanyl in LaPorte County, Indiana.</p><p>Akison, of Romeoville, was making Amazon deliveries at the time of the crash and was sentenced to eight years in prison. Akison pleaded guilty to causing catastrophic injury when operating a motor vehicle while under the influence and causing serious bodily harm while operating a motor vehicle under the influence, officials said. </p><p>But Bradshaw's family says the driver wasn't the only one responsible and is seeking to hold others accountable.</p><p>A civil lawsuit, filed last week in LaPorte County Superior Court, is accusing Amazon and other defendants of negligence for failing to remove Akison – who allegedly had a history of reckless driving and drug use – as a driver.</p><p>“This isn’t just Luca’s story, this is about everybody,” Bradley Bradshaw, Lucas’ father, said Thursday morning at a news conference at a Loop law firm. “If these are controllable things that don't need to happen, let's make some changes.”</p><p>Bradley Bradshaw, a volunteer coach, was driving the bus the day of the crash. He was pulling up to a stop light and when he looked at the rearview mirror he realized they were seconds away from being hit.</p><p>“Every time I look in a rearview mirror I see the truck,” said Bradshaw. “It's one thing I'm never going to get out of my mind.”</p><p>Five players and two coaches including Lucas' dad were on the bus, and most suffered injuries. But Lucas Bradshaw was the most seriously hurt. He was ejected from the bus during the crash and knocked unconscious after landing several feet away.</p><p>He was airlifted to a hospital and suffered a traumatic brain injury, multiple brain bleeds, multiple facial fractures, a fractured arm, and other injuries. He was in a coma for about 60 days following the crash and was hospitalized and in intense therapies for more than 125 days, his family said.</p><p>Even more than a year after the crash, Lucas is still working to recover. He still has issues with his vision in his left eye, his walk is different and is mentally slow to respond.</p><p>“If you were to watch him, his gait, how he walks, you might say that he had a stroke,” said Kelly Bradshaw, Lucas' mother.</p><p>The crash changed nearly every part of Lucas Bradshaw’s life. He missed his junior year of high school, stepped away from baseball and could no longer lend a hand on his family’s Indiana farm.</p><p>Attorneys representing the family said the crash could have been prevented.</p><p>The lawsuit names Amazon, Elite Courier, Enterprise Leasing Company, St. Joseph County and Akison as defendants. Akison was contracted through Elite Courier, hauling Amazon deliveries when the crash occurred.</p><p>Amazon argued that Akison was not an employee of Amazon.</p><p>“This was a tragedy, and our hearts are with the families affected as they recover and the entire LaPorte County community. Given this is active litigation, we have no further comment,” Amazon said in a statement.</p><p>But labels don’t matter, said Nick Kamenjarin, an attorney representing the family.</p><p>“What matters is the control,” he said. “Amazon controlled virtually every aspect of Mr. Akison's job. They monitored his performance, his safety, and they retained the authority to suspend him from the program, as well as terminating from the program.”</p><p>Kamenjarin said Amazon contracted with Elite Courier and provided Akison access to the company's driver app, which is used to assign routes, coordinate pickups and track drivers' locations.</p><p>The family is also suing St. Joseph County, alleging a county officer attempted to stop Akison after receiving reports of his erratic driving but ended the pursuit when Akison crossed the county line. Akison crashed into the bus shortly after.</p><p>According to the lawsuit, St. Joseph County officials never notified LaPorte County, where the crash occurred, that Akison had entered their jurisdiction or that his driving posed a potential threat.</p><p>St. Joseph County did not immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Lucas Bradshaw will return to in-person classes for his senior year in the Fall. His parents said Lucas hopes to return to playing baseball and helping with the crops at the farm.</p><p>Despite all of their struggles, the family said they were grateful for the community's support.</p><p>“We cannot thank our community enough,” said Bradley Bradshaw. “It wasn’t just our family fighting the fight. It was a community fight. I’s been Team Lucas all the way.”<br></p>

entries.title: Aurora emite advertencia sobre agua con plomo después de que algunas casas superan los niveles
entries.summary: <p>Aurora emitió una advertencia el martes luego de que funcionarios reportaran niveles de plomo “elevados” en el agua potable de algunos hogares de la ciudad.</p><p>La Ciudad aconseja a los residentes que usen filtros para el agua de la llave y que hagan pruebas a los niños para detectar la exposición al plomo, aunque especifica que los niveles corresponden a “plomo encontrado en hogares calificados específicos que participan en el programa de muestreo”, y no a toda la ciudad.</p><p>Los residentes cuyos hogares dieron positivo fueron contactados y la Ciudad publicó un <a class="Link" href="https://yourvoice.aurora.il.us/leadnotice" target="_blank" >mapa de las líneas de servicio afectadas</a>, según se indicó en <a class="Link" href="https://www.aurora.il.us/News-articles/Lead-Action-Level-Exceedance-Notice" target="_blank" >la alerta</a>.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-610000" name="module-610000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El aviso, emitido el martes, señaló que las líneas de servicio de plomo eran las responsables y que entre enero y junio de este año la División de Protección del Agua de la ciudad encontró que más del 10% de las 100 muestras recogidas excedieron el “nivel de acción para el plomo” establecido por la Agencia de Protección Ambiental (EPA).</p><p>Las lecturas hacen que la Ciudad sea responsable de “la educación pública, el ajuste del tratamiento y el reemplazo de las líneas de servicio de plomo”.</p><p>“El nivel de acción de plomo es una medida de la efectividad del tratamiento de control de la corrosión en los sistemas de agua”, dijo la Ciudad. “El nivel de acción no es un estándar para establecer un nivel seguro de plomo en un hogar… [y] esto no significa que cada propiedad que recibe agua potable de la División de Producción de Agua de la Ciudad de Aurora tenga plomo en el agua potable”.</p><p>El plomo es especialmente dañino para los niños con cerebros en desarrollo y puede causar una serie de condiciones de salud graves en los adultos. El plomo puede dañar el cerebro y el sistema nervioso, así como provocar crecimiento lento y dificultades en el desarrollo, el comportamiento y el aprendizaje, según el Departamento de Salud de Illinois (IDPH).</p><p>El año pasado, alrededor de <a class="Link" href="https://dph.illinois.gov/topics-services/environmental-health-protection/lead-poisoning-prevention/families-of-lead-exposed-children/pediatric-highrisk-zip-codes.html" target="_blank" >180 códigos postales</a> en 47 condados, o aproximadamente el 13% del estado, fueron añadidos a una lista del departamento de salud estatal que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/07/10/lead-exposure-testing-illinois" target="_blank" >requiere que los niños sean sometidos a pruebas de exposición al plomo</a>.</p><p>“La exposición al plomo en el agua potable puede causar efectos graves en la salud en todos los grupos de edad”, advertía la Ciudad.</p><p>Los filtros certificados para eliminar plomo, etiquetados como Norma NSF/ANSI 53, y partículas, etiquetados como Norma NSF/ANSI 42, pueden ayudar a <a class="Link" href="https://dph.illinois.gov/topics-services/environmental-health-protection/lead-in-water.html" target="_blank" >reducir la exposición</a>, según el departamento de salud estatal.</p><p>Los residentes también pueden hacer que su agua sea sometida a pruebas y limpiar los filtros de sus fregaderos, entre otras medidas preventivas, aunque hervir el agua no elimina el plomo.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Groundswell Coffee to open in historic Fine Arts Building
entries.summary: <p>Within the Fine Arts Building, sounds such as pianos and opera singing drifting through its corridors are part of its atmospheric aura. Soon, the aroma of brewing coffee will add to the sensory mix.</p><p>Groundswell Coffee Roasters is expected to open in the Fine Arts Building next week — pending final city inspections — marking the first cafe in the Downtown architectural landmark since its Artist’s Cafe closed in 2019.</p><p>“We’ve been waiting for this for quite some time,” painter and art teacher Don Yang said at a preview for tenants last week.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f20000" building 13 years ago. He expects his students will stop by the cafe, and parents who drop off children for lessons will have a place to wait.</p><p>Groundswell will open daily from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. to serve building tenants, as well as local college students and visitors. The cafe, 410 S. Michigan Ave., spans about 1,000 square feet and will offer food and beverages.</p><p>Fine Arts Building tenants include more than 140 visual artists, musicians, writers, dancers and small businesses such as psychologists and a yoga studio, as well as organizations such as the Jazz Institute of Chicago. The 10-story building is also home to the Studebaker Theater where NPR does live tapings of quiz show “Wait Wait… Don’t Tell Me!”</p><p>Since the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/entertainment-and-culture/2023/10/11/23912151/fine-arts-building-125th-anniversary-chicago" >Fine Arts Building</a> opened in 1898, tenants have included architect Frank Lloyd Wright and Wizard of Oz illustrator William Denslow.</p><p>Groundswell’s launch continues a revitalization for the building, including a multimillion-dollar restoration of the Studebaker Theater from 2021 to 2023.</p><p>More plans are ahead. The building expects to eventually open a restaurant in the storefront vacated by the Artist’s Cafe, Jacob Harvey, Fine Arts Building’s managing artistic director, said.</p><div class="Enhancement" Both are Fine Arts Building tenants.</p><p>Hammersley Architecture previously worked on the Studebaker Theater’s renovation. The cafe shares design motifs with the Studebaker, such as wood paneling and metal grating found in the theater.</p><p>Groundswell’s contemporary decor retains the art deco vibe of the Fine Arts Building. The cafe features patterned wall tiles, light fixtures similar to ones in studios and a gilt-framed mirror from an elevator originally in the space.</p><p>The Fine Arts Building was created from the former Studebaker Carriage Co. headquarters, which originally built and displayed carriages there from 1887.</p><p>While retail and office vacancies in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/04/08/civic-leaders-chicago-loop-alliance-state-street" target="_blank" ><u>Loop remain high</u></a>, the building is 98% occupied and is “alive and thriving,” Harvey said. There is a long wait list for potential tenants.</p><p>And the number of visitors is growing. Last year, the Studebaker Theater had more than 70,000 patrons. More are expected this year, Harvey said.</p><p>The building hosts open studios on the second Friday of the month. Five years ago, the event drew about 40 visitors. Now, more than 500 come, Harvey said. entries.title: Amazon receives first city approvals for Gage Park distribution center
entries.summary: <p>Amazon’s plans for its latest last mile distribution center — the fourth in Chicago — took a major step forward Thursday.</p><p>The Chicago Plan Commission gave the first city approval for Amazon's 235,137-square-foot last mile center at the former Central Steel & Wire plant, 3000 W. 51st St. Amazon purchased the site in 2021 for $35 million — one of its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2021/7/14/22577872/amazon-buys-sw-side-property-for-35-million" >biggest land deals</a> in Chicago at the time.</p><p>Amazon’s last mile centers are the final stop in the delivery process before packages arrive at customers’ doors. It also has three other last mile centers in the city, including a Bridgeport location that opened July 2025. At the time, the Bridgeport facility employed about 150.</p><p>Amazon has four operations sites with one in Bridgeport, Back of the Yards, Pullman and West Humboldt Park, according to the company. It also has a distribution hub in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2021/4/7/22372242/amazon-online-retailer-working-conditions-protest-walkout-gage-park-facility" >Gage Park</a>.</p><p>The new facility will give Gage Park residents “better, faster, more efficient deliveries,” Kyle DeGuilio, senior manager of economic development policy for Amazon, said.</p><p>The development team emphasized the facility will take up three acres on the roughly 69-acre site, with “generous setbacks.” The facility would be at least one football field length, or 360 feet, away from bordering streets. The CTA Orange Line is north of the property.</p><p>“We are taking a property that has been fully industrial since the late '30s … and replacing it with a low-profile, heavily landscaped facility that is greatly about ... open space,” said Jeff Cali, senior vice president of development services at Venture One Real Estate. Venture One is developing the property on behalf of Amazon.</p><p>Also on the site will be 244 parking spaces and a 4,500-square-foot fleet service building with three loading bays. The development team said most vehicles, including delivery trucks, will arrive and leave outside of rush hour in order to reduce the traffic impact on neighbors. Traffic and pedestrian safety were two of neighbors’ top concerns with the proposed facility, according to Ald. Jeylú Gutiérrez (14th).</p><p>Amazon plans to do “significant landscaping” at the site, including trees around the lot’s perimeter to shield it from neighbors, according to its presentation to the commission. Two acres on the southeast corner of the site will also be donated to the Chicago Park District to keep as open space, Cali said. Gutiérrez’s office said Amazon has committed to paying for the development of the park space.</p><p>“Over the past several months, I've been in regular communications with Amazon. I appreciate their willingness to listen, engage and recognize that they are coming into a community that has been historically been underserved and too often overlooked for investment,” Gutiérrez wrote in a letter of support for the project. “I look forward to continuing to work with Amazon to ensure this investment benefits both the residents of the 14th Ward and the company for years to come.”</p><p>If approved, Amazon hopes to start construction in October, with a September 2027 completion.</p><p>The development would create about 350 temporary construction jobs. Once operational, Amazon said it will employ roughly 200 employees. Hourly wages would start at $21.50, with benefits. An additional 400 jobs for delivery service partners would be added.</p>

entries.title: Photo of man who allegedly tried to lure girl in Norwood Park released by police
entries.summary: <p>Police released a picture of a man who allegedly tried to lure a 13-year-old girl from a front porch in Norwood Park last week.</p><p>The girl was sitting on the porch in the 6200 block of North Naper Avenue about 6:30 p.m. on July 10 when a person only described as a male who was delivering packages approached her and asked, "Do you want to make some extra money?" police said. </p><p>When the girl asked what he was talking about, he repeated his question, adding, "I can show you on my phone; follow me," causing the girl to go back into her home, police said. </p><p>Anyone with information should contact Area 5 detectives at 312-746-6554 or submit an anonymous tip at CPDTIP.com and use reference No. JK329235. <br><b> </b></p>

entries.title: City Council deadline to accept or reject parking meter deal extended until Sept. 30
entries.summary: <p>The City Council now has until Sept. 30 to either approve a New York investment firm’s $2.53 billion bid to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/05/18/chicagos-parking-meters-could-be-sold-again-under-deal-requiring-city-council-approval" >acquire Chicago parking meters</a> or risk a lawsuit by the current owner that has more than recouped its initial investment with 57 years remaining on the deal.</p><p>Finance Committee Chair Pat Dowell (3rd) told her colleagues late Wednesday she was informed that the revised July 24 deadline had been extended for nine weeks by Mark Rotatori, a partner at Jones Day, the law firm retained by the Law Department to advise the City Council on the offer from Stonepeak Partners.</p><p>It’s the second time that Chicago Parking Meters LLC, a consortium that includes Morgan Stanley, Allianz Capital Partners and the Sovereign Wealth Fund of Abu Dhabi, has agreed to extend the deadline to approve its proposal to sell the 57 years remaining on the 75-year lease to Stonepeak Partners. The original deadline was June 30 and was extended until July 24.</p><p>It’s not clear whether the renewed flexibility came from the seller, the owners or both.</p><p></p><p>Asked at a June 25 Finance Committee hearing what would happen if the deadline was not met or if the City Council rejected the sale, James Wyper, senior managing director for Stonepeak Partners, told committee members, “You’ll never see me again. We get all the money. I’m going. It’s OK. What Morgan Stanley and the existing ownership group choose to do does not involve me at all. They’ll probably sue you.”</p><p>Former U.S. Attorney Dan Webb, an attorney representing the current owner, could not be reached for comment.</p><p>In a July 3 letter to Mayor Brandon Johnson, Dowell warned that the proposal by Chicago Parking Meters LLC to unload the parking meter deal “has not secured the support necessary to advance from committee at this time.”</p><p>“Significant questions remain regarding Stonepeak’s ownership structure, regulatory and legal history, operational practices and the potential implications of this transfer for the city of Chicago as outlined in the June 11 Chicago City Council Position letter to Stonepeak” signed by 15 City Council members, Dowell wrote.</p><p>“These are fundamental considerations for any legislative body asked to approve the transfer of a public asset of this magnitude.”</p><p>To avoid almost certain defeat, Dowell <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/13/finance-committee-stalls-showdown-vote-on-sale-of-chicago-parking-meters" >postponed a showdown vote </a>at Monday’s Finance Committee meeting.</p><p>The extension until Sept. 30 buys more time for Budget Committee Chair Jason Ervin (28th), Johnson's most powerful City Council ally, to push his long-shot alternative plan.</p><p>Ervin wants to to create a public infrastructure trust similar to the one created, then abandoned by former Mayor Rahm Emanuel to acquire the parking meters, using a mix of investments by the four city employee pension funds and municipal bonds.</p><p>“That was then. This is now. We have a meaningful asset that can be utilized and it also potentially strengthens our pension funds and it works to bring that value back to Chicagoans — not let the money go halfway around the world,” Ervin told the Sun-Times this week. “Other pension funds are investing in this. Why wouldn’t we afford that same opportunity to our four pension funds in the city of Chicago?”</p><p>Johnson ultimately abandoned his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/brandon-johnson/2026/07/10/johnson-finally-explains-his-decision-to-bid-3-2b-for-parking-meters-before-walking-away" >$3.2 billion bid </a>to take back Chicago parking meters after determining that the risk of undoing the parking meter deal was not worth the reward — either financially or politically.</p><p>It would have required pledging to siphon other major sources of revenue the city depends on “if parking habits shifted, alternative modes of transportation become more common” and “driver/commuter behaviors” changed.</p><p>That’s a possibility amid a fast-changing landscape for parking demand that includes everything from self-driving vehicles and robot deliveries to congestion fees that discourage people from driving Downtown.</p><p>Against that backdrop, Ervin was asked Monday to explain how he would bankroll the proposed Infrastructure trust purchase.</p><p>“There would definitely need to be some financing done by the city. … Looking at all options, that would probably include pension obligation bonds, general obligation bonds. Even maybe some revenue bonds along TIF and other things,” Ervin said. “It’s just an opportunity that we need to explore — we need to look at — and not let this opportunity pass us by."</p><p>Johnson said he appreciated Ervin’s creative thinking. But during an appearance Thursday on the WBEZ program “Ask the Mayor,” Johnson again refused to say whether the City Council should accept or reject Stonepeak’s offer to purchase the meter system for $700 million less than the city’s “last, best” offer.</p><p>"The authority rests solely with the City Council. That is their decision," the mayor said.</p>

entries.title: White Sox entering uncharted territory, from general manager Chris Getz on down
entries.summary: <p>General manager Chris Getz and manager Will Venable already have gotten the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> from Point A to Point B, a destination no one thought they’d reach so soon. Now they’ll have to get them to Point C without hurting their chances of reaching other points down the road.</p><p>Otherwise, this whole exercise could be pointless.</p><p>The Sox return from the All-Star break Friday against the Blue Jays, who have been the opposite of the Sox, falling to last place in the American League East after winning the division and reaching the World Series last season. The Sox have gone from worst to first in the Central, and staying there in the final 67 games will be even harder than it was getting there.</p><p>“There’s going to be unique situations hopefully, spots that these guys haven’t been in before with a good record, playing meaningful games down the stretch,” Venable said this week. “We’ll figure it out when we get there, but these guys have handled everything great to this point. [We’re] looking forward to whatever challenges lie ahead in the second half.”</p><p>Getz’s biggest challenge will be improving the team without sacrificing too much of what he has built since taking the helm Aug. 31, 2023. The Sox entered 2025 with the sixth-ranked farm system in the majors, according to MLB.com. After several promotions dropped it to 16th entering this season, Getz replenished the system with a highly touted draft class.</p><p>Fans will watch Getz work in a way they never have: from a position of strength and with a playoff spot in sight. But he’ll have to be realistic about his team’s chances in the postseason, even in a down year for the AL. Is making a splash before the trade deadline worth it, or is Getz better off waiting another season, after the farm system develops more talent to play or trade?</p><p>But next season might not even happen. Owners and players are already lined up for a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/mlb/2026/07/15/mlb-labor-negotiations-mlbpa-lockout-strike-salary-cap" >possibly catastrophic labor war.</a> Does that push Getz to strike while the iron is hot? Seasons like the one the Sox are having are precious, and failing to take full advantage might send a bad message to the clubhouse, which has had a utopian environment.</p><p>“We just keep trying to get better. That’s the focus for us,” Venable said. “We do have a lot of young guys. We have a lot of guys who are still learning every day. I’m learning every day. I think we’re all excited to do it together. That’s what it’s going to be about down the stretch.”</p><p>Indeed it will, and more than anything Getz does or doesn’t do, that inexperience could lead to the Sox’ undoing. As well as they’ve played, most of them haven’t encountered what they’re about to: a pennant race. Plays that were made in June can become harder to make in September, when the pressure turns up.</p><p>The Sox showed the potential to handle that this month, when they bounced back from two gut-punch, walk-off losses to split a four-game series with the Guardians, with whom they’re tied for first in the Central. They’ll need more of that mental fortitude not just to hold off the Guardians, but the Twins, who are only three games back.</p><p>And as Venable said, he’s learning, too. The Sox have a potentially lethal mix of inexperience on the field and in the dugout. Venable has stuck to his guns on leaning into hitters’ handedness in matchups and using his bullpen by committee. Both have largely worked, but using relievers in different roles and for multiple innings could leave the bullpen short when it’s needed most.</p><p>So much to learn, and so many points to reach.</p><h3>On deck</h3><p><b>SOX AT BLUE JAYS</b></p><p><b>Friday:</b> Anthony Kay (6-4, 4.23 ERA) vs. Spencer Miles (4-1, 2.85), 6:15 p.m., Apple TV, 1000-AM.</p><p><b>Saturday:</b> Davis Martin (9-4, 3.41) vs. Shane Bieber (0-1, 7.64), 2:07 p.m., CHSN, 1000-AM.</p><p><b>Sunday:</b> Sean Burke (6-4, 3.41) vs. Trey Yesavage (4-4, 3.72), 11:15 a.m., NBCSN, Peacock, 1000-AM.</p><div
